On Saturday nights Hana Rourke worked the coat check at the Belmont Hotel, a closet off the ballroom with three rails of numbered hangers and a half door she could lean on between rushes. The job paid nine dollars an hour plus whatever guests dropped into a glass jar on the counter. Mr. Esposito, the banquet manager, had taped three rules inside the half door in black marker: ONE TICKET, ONE COAT. STAY OUT OF THE POCKETS. A COAT WITHOUT A TICKET WAITS UNTIL THE ROOM IS EMPTY.

Hana had decided by her second Saturday that the third rule was meant for a hotel much larger than the Belmont. At a wedding of a hundred guests, she told her friend Dev, she could match nearly every face to its coat. She had tested herself, silently, as people came back for their things, and she had been right every time.

The wedding that Saturday was larger than a hundred. Between seven and seven-twenty, forty coats came over the half door, most of them black, and Hana stopped looking at faces. She looked at hands, at tickets, at the hook of each hanger as she hung it, and she tore stubs so fast that the counter was white with paper.

At a quarter past ten a man in a gray suit leaned on the half door, patting his jacket. He had lost his ticket, he said, and his babysitter had to be home by eleven. He pointed past her shoulder. "That one. The long one with the belt, at forty-one."

Hana turned. There was a long black coat with a belt on hanger 41. There was another on hanger 44, and she could not have said which of them had come from his hands. Both had arrived in the rush. She thought of what she had told Dev, and her face grew warm.

"I'm sorry," she said. "You'll have to wait until the room clears."

The man looked at her for a long moment. Then he sat down on the bench by the elevator and called someone on his phone, and he did not raise his voice, which was somehow worse.

At ten-forty a woman in a green dress handed Hana ticket 41. Hana lifted the belted coat from hanger 41, held it while the woman found the sleeves, and watched her button it to the collar. On the bench the man had half risen to his feet. He sat back down.

When the room emptied at half past eleven, one long black coat was left on the rails. The man put it on without a word, walked to the elevator, then came back and pushed a folded bill into the jar. Hana waited until the elevator doors had closed before she looked at it. Then she went to the half door and pressed flat the corner of the tape, which had begun to curl.

My uncle Teodor cooked at a restaurant on Grand Avenue for twenty-two years, and on Sunday mornings, when the kitchen was closed, he sharpened its knives at our kitchen table. The summer I was fourteen I asked him to teach me, mostly because the restaurant paid him forty dollars for the job and I had calculated that I could do it in half the time.

He set a whetstone in a wet towel so that it would sit still, and he handed me the oldest knife in the roll, a chef's knife with a chip near the heel. Then he took it back and showed me the angle: the spine lifted about the height of two stacked coins. "Hold that," he said, "the whole way, every stroke, both sides." I held it for perhaps six strokes before my wrist began to drift, and I heard the change before I saw it, a dull scrape where there had been a whisper.

What he wanted me to find was the burr. If you grind one side of an edge long enough, a thin curl of steel folds over onto the other side, too fine to see. You find it with the pad of your thumb, drawn gently across the edge, never along it. Until you can feel the burr along the whole length of the blade, he said, the side is unfinished, however long you have been at it.

I spent most of July on that first knife. I would grind for ten minutes, feel nothing, grind for ten more, and hand it to him in triumph, and he would draw his thumb across the edge and hand it back. Once I tried to speed things up by pressing harder. The stone grabbed, the knife skated off the end, and I spent the next hour on a scratch I had put there myself. I was fairly sure, at fourteen, that the burr was something he had invented to keep the forty dollars.

In the first week of August I felt it: a faint roughness, like a hair caught on the edge, running from heel to tip. I made him feel it twice. He nodded, showed me how to turn the knife over and take the burr off with lighter strokes, and then slid a sheet of newspaper toward me. The knife went down through it from the top edge without a sound.

That fall he let me do the paring knives, which the restaurant hardly used, and in December he gave me five dollars of the forty. I believe I told everyone at school that I was in the knife business.

I still sharpen my own knives, and when friends ask how long it takes, I tell them the truth, which is that I have no idea. It takes until the burr.

Many families who own a copy of Monopoly agree on two things: the game takes forever, and it often ends with someone quitting rather than losing. Many of the same families play with a rule that appears nowhere in the printed instructions. Taxes and fines go into the middle of the board instead of to the bank, and whoever lands on Free Parking collects the pile.

The printed rules are plain about that corner. Free Parking is a resting space, and a player who lands there collects nothing at all.

The house rule feels generous, and that is exactly its trouble. Monopoly is designed to end. Players are supposed to run out of money one by one, and the last player left with money wins. Every dollar in the Free Parking pile is a dollar that would have left the game, handed back to a lucky player instead. A family that pays out a few hundred dollars from the middle every few turns has, in effect, built a pump that keeps nearly bankrupt players alive. The game's ending was never broken; the family switched it off.

A second habit works the same way. The official rules say that when a player lands on an unowned property and declines to buy it, the bank auctions it at once, and any player may bid, including the one who declined. Many households skip the auction because it seems like a fuss. Without it, properties sit unsold for trip after trip around the board, color groups take far longer to complete, and the high rents that would bring the game to a close arrive late, or after everyone has drifted off to dinner.

It is worth asking why these two habits have spread so widely. Both soften the game for whoever is losing. Collecting the pile feels like luck rewarding the unlucky, and skipping the auction spares a cautious player the pressure of bidding against a sibling. They are kind rules, invented by people who wanted everyone at the table to stay in.

But a game's rules are an agreement about what will happen, including what will happen at the end. Changing one changes the agreement. That is a fair thing to do, as long as a family knows what it is trading away. Most do not. They blame the box for a long evening and keep the pile under the board, where it has been all along, doing exactly what they put it there to do.

Many families who own a copy of Monopoly agree on two things: the game takes forever, and it often ends with someone quitting rather than losing. Many of the same families play with a rule that appears nowhere in the printed instructions. Taxes and fines go into the middle of the board instead of to the bank, and whoever lands on Free Parking collects the pile.

The printed rules are plain about that corner. Free Parking is a resting space, and a player who lands there collects nothing at all.

The house rule feels generous, and that is exactly its trouble. Monopoly is designed to end. Players are supposed to run out of money one by one, and the last player left with money wins. Every dollar in the Free Parking pile is a dollar that would have left the game, handed back to a lucky player instead. A family that pays out a few hundred dollars from the middle every few turns has, in effect, built a pump that keeps nearly bankrupt players alive. The game's ending was never broken; the family switched it off.

A second habit works the same way. The official rules say that when a player lands on an unowned property and declines to buy it, the bank auctions it at once, and any player may bid, including the one who declined. Many households skip the auction because it seems like a fuss. Without it, properties sit unsold for trip after trip around the board, color groups take far longer to complete, and the high rents that would bring the game to a close arrive late, or after everyone has drifted off to dinner.

It is worth asking why these two habits have spread so widely. Both soften the game for whoever is losing. Collecting the pile feels like luck rewarding the unlucky, and skipping the auction spares a cautious player the pressure of bidding against a sibling. They are kind rules, invented by people who wanted everyone at the table to stay in.

But a game's rules are an agreement about what will happen, including what will happen at the end. Changing one changes the agreement. That is a fair thing to do, as long as a family knows what it is trading away. Most do not. They blame the box for a long evening and keep the pile under the board, where it has been all along, doing exactly what they put it there to do.

item.passage:
In the 1880s the town of Pell's Crossing had no official ballot. A voter brought his own: a slip of paper printed with his party's candidates, which he dropped into a glass-sided box at the schoolhouse while his neighbors looked on. The parties paid to have these slips, called tickets, printed by the thousand, and the only press in Pell's Crossing able to print them belonged to Owen Tisdale, who also printed the weekly Crossing Register.

Tisdale printed tickets for both parties, the Farmers' Union and the Citizens, and for a dozen years the work was routine. In the late summer of 1886 the Citizens' committee brought him an order with an unusual instruction. Their tickets were to be printed on bright pink paper, which the committee had bought itself and carried to the shop in bundles.

Tisdale understood the purpose at once. A pink ticket could be recognized from across the schoolhouse, and so could the man holding it. Several members of the committee owned the mills and stores where half the town's voters worked, and a clerk or a mill hand who walked to the box with a white ticket would be seen doing it.

He sent the pink paper back. He would print the Citizens' tickets, he wrote, on the same white stock and in the same size of type as the Union's, as he always had, and at the same price. The committee took its order to a printer in Garland, eighteen miles away, and withdrew its advertising from the Register. That advertising had covered roughly a third of the paper's costs, and that winter Tisdale sold one of his two presses.

The election that fall was held with pink tickets and white ones dropping side by side into the glass box. The Citizens won by a wider margin than in any year before, and few people in town doubted the reason.

Five years later the legislature required every town in the state to use a single official ballot, printed at public expense, listing every candidate on one sheet, and marked by each voter alone in a curtained booth. The county clerk needed a printer for the ballots of Pell's Crossing and gave the work to Tisdale. On the first election day under the new law, the glass box was gone from the schoolhouse. In its place stood a box of plain pine, with a slot in the lid just wide enough for a folded sheet.

item.passage:
In 2009, doctors in Japan described a yeast that had never been recorded before, taken from the ear of a single patient. They named it Candida auris, from the Latin word for ear, and for a few years it was a minor entry in the medical literature.

Then it began turning up in hospitals: in India and Pakistan, in South Africa, in Venezuela, often in patients who were already seriously ill and often in the bloodstream. Many samples resisted fluconazole, the drug doctors most often use against yeast infections, and some resisted two or three classes of antifungal drugs. Routine laboratory tests frequently mistook it for other, more familiar yeasts, so for a time hospitals that had it may have been recording something else.

The obvious explanation was that a single strain had spread from one place, carried by patients and travelers from hospital to hospital. A team led by scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tested that idea by reading the complete genetic code of samples from several of those countries. If one strain had spread, samples from different continents should have been nearly identical. Samples from within a single region were. Between regions, the samples differed by tens of thousands of small genetic changes, far too many to have built up in a few years. The yeast had arisen separately in Asia, in Africa, and in South America, at roughly the same time.

The idea remains a hypothesis, and its authors present it as one.

It survives for weeks on bed rails and other hospital surfaces, and on the skin of patients who seem perfectly well, which lets it pass quietly from one bed to the next. Some hospitals that found it have had to close entire wards for cleaning. Doctors are used to yeast infections that start from a patient's own body. In 2009, doctors in Japan described a yeast that had never been recorded before, taken from the ear of a single patient. They named it Candida auris, from the Latin word for ear, and for a few years it was a minor entry in the medical literature.

Then it began turning up in hospitals: in India and Pakistan, in South Africa, in Venezuela, often in patients who were already seriously ill and often in the bloodstream. Many samples resisted fluconazole, the drug doctors most often use against yeast infections, and some resisted two or three classes of antifungal drugs. Routine laboratory tests frequently mistook it for other, more familiar yeasts, so for a time hospitals that had it may have been recording something else.

The obvious explanation was that a single strain had spread from one place, carried by patients and travelers from hospital to hospital. A team led by scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tested that idea by reading the complete genetic code of samples from several of those countries. If one strain had spread, samples from different continents should have been nearly identical. Samples from within a single region were. Between regions, the samples differed by tens of thousands of small genetic changes, far too many to have built up in a few years. The yeast had arisen separately in Asia, in Africa, and in South America, at roughly the same time.

That is worse news than a single traveling strain would have been. A strain that spreads outward from one hospital can, at least in principle, be traced back and stopped at its source. A yeast that appears on three continents within a few years suggests that something shared by all of them has changed, and that the same change may be at work in places where the yeast has yet to be found. One proposal, published in 2019, is that a warming climate has pushed some fungi in the wild to tolerate higher temperatures, closer to the heat of the human body, which has long protected people from most fungi. The idea remains a hypothesis, and its authors present it as one.

Meanwhile the yeast does something unusual for its kind. It survives for weeks on bed rails and other hospital surfaces, and on the skin of patients who seem perfectly well, which lets it pass quietly from one bed to the next. Some hospitals that found it have had to close entire wards for cleaning. Doctors are used to yeast infections that start from a patient's own body. This one behaves more like a contagious bacterium, and the genetic record says it could begin almost anywhere.
